newsitem.title: KENYA: African leaders back down on sanctions on Burundi.
newsitem.headline: African leaders back down on sanctions on Burundi.

text.p: Even Kenya's foreign minister found it hard on Thursday to adjust to the elevation of Burundi military ruler Pierre Buyoya to the rank of "president" by regional leaders.
Kalonzo Musyoka at a Nairobi news briefing noted the official change and then interspersed President Buyoya with Mr Buyoya and once said: "President, err, Mr, Buyoya".
The confusion was understandable 24 hours after leaders who clamped sanctions on landlocked Burundi nine months ago eased them greatly and recognised the Tutsi military ruler as president.

Asked how the leaders could recognise as president a man who seized power in an army coup and had not met their demands, Musyoka said he thought the title was "subject to negotiation" but also reflected the need to recognise reality in Burundi.

The reality was that sweeping sanctions simply were not working. In fact the leaders bought Buyoya's argument that they were only hurting the poor and were fuelling extremism among the 15 percent Tutsi minority.
Fuel and food for aid agencies were already exempted from sanctions imposed on July 31, six days after the army ousted Hutu President Sylvestre Ntibantunganya and installed Buyoya.
"The killings continue but the positive thing is that Mr Buyoya seems to have shown a boldness to take the bull by the horns and to begin some kind of discussion," Musyoka said.

"We hope therefore that President Buyoya...will now be able to very seriously do the three things that were required of him: unban political parties, restore parliament and undertake unconditional negotiations with all parties to the conflict."
Buyoya, a retired army major and president of the tiny African country for the second time, has repeatedly said he is ready to negotiate with Hutu rebels but talks have not begun.

The result of the regional summit on Wednesday in the northern Tanzanian town of Arusha was a victory for Buyoya, especially since Musyoka said the leaders were told more than 50,000 people had been killed in Burundi since the coup.

Before the army takeover the U.N. estimate was that 150,000 people had been killed in massacres and fighting between the army and rebels since army units murdered Burundi's first freely elected president, Melchior Ndadaye, in 1993.
Some diplomats have recently spoken of fears of a coup against Buyoya by hardline Tutsi army officers opposed to any talks with Hutu rebel leader Leonard Nyangoma.

The capital has been hit in recent weeks by a series of mine blasts following what authorities said was the arrest of a group plotting to assassinate Buyoya. They said the group included supporters of another former Tutsi military ruler, Jean-Baptiste Bagaza.
"Nobody wants to be punitive on Burundi, nobody wants to be seen to be hard on the suffering people," said Kenya's Musyoka.

"What the leaders are telling him is no one wants to continue imposing sanctions as everyone knows how unpopular the whole subject of imposing sanctions is...but the leaders also want to see peace and stability in the country."
Sanctions were imposed on Burundi because regional leaders wanted to make clear that the days of army coups were over. But the wider international community failed to endorse them.
Buyoya, credited for handing power to Ndadaye in 1993, played on those fears while smugglers ignored the embargo.

In the meantime the army went on the offensive against Hutu rebels after their main bases in eastern Zaire and supply lines were destroyed by the Tutsi-dominated rebellion which began there last October.
U.N. diplomats however still have deep doubts about Buyoya's willingness to sit at the negotiating table with Nyangoma.
